newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian union row casts shadow over wage talks.
newsitem.headline: Italian union row casts shadow over wage talks.

text.p: A bitter row has broken out in the Italian labour movement over how to increase employment in the crisis-hit south of the country, casting a shadow over crucial wage talks between metal workers' unions and their employers.

Leaders of the powerful CISL union confederation representing Italy's poor south said last week they were prepared to negotiate lower starting salaries than in the prosperous north in order to boost employment.
Sergio D'Antoni, the national secretary of the Catholic-inspired CISL, immediately threw his weight behind the proposals at the weekend.

"We want to bring investment to areas with high joblessness by allowing a reduction in contractual salaries for three to four years so that it is attractive for companies to invest in the south," D'Antoni told the Turin daily La Stampa on Sunday.
"It is better to be employed, even with a lower salary in the early years than to remain jobless," D'Antoni said.
Until now nationwide labour contracts have bound employers who take on staff in the south of the country -- where unemployment is rampant -- on the same terms that apply in the prosperous north.
Many employers, particularly in smaller companies, have got round these restriction by illegally hiring casual labour without any binding contract.
D'Antoni's remarks drew plaudits from employers but brought down the wrath of the leaders of two rival nationwide labour confederations, CGIL and UIL.

"Of course new jobs are needed in the south but it is wrong to propose lower salaries in order to create these jobs. It is an old, illusory idea," said Sergio Cofferati, leader of the CGIL. UIL leader Pietro Larizza was even more scornful of the idea, saying "the southern colleagues are showing remarkable ingenuousness if they think the (unemployment) problem can be solved in this way."
A left-wing economist, Paolo Sylos Labini, said he was puzzled by the strength of union opposition to the idea of introducing lower starting salaries in the south.
"Sometimes trade unions are stronger in defending those who already have jobs than those who are still looking for them," Milan daily Corriere della Sera quoted Labini as saying.
The angry exchanges among top union leaders came at a delicate moment in stalled negotiations between engineering and metal workers' unions and their employers.
Unions representing 1.7 million workers in the sector last week agreed to launch a wave of strikes to back their claims for higher wages to cover the 1996-98 contract period.
The unions have been locked in a dispute with employers since July over renewal of the two-year rolling contract which expired in the middle of last year.
The main engineering employers' association, Federmeccanica, has publicly rejected a government suggestion that workers should be given 200,000 lire ($129) a month to cover the new contract period.

But newspapers reported on Sunday that Federmeccanica was condidering whether to accept the government proposals on condition that the contract ran for two-and-a-half years -- six months longer than the old one.

Pressure has been mounting on Federmeccanica to accept a compromise after a number of employers in northeast Italy broke ranks and signed deals with unions granting the 200,000 lire monthly increase suggested by the government.
